stories.headline: Nvidia scandal deepens: Huang resigns, Lutnick faces pressure, both summoned to testify

claims.text: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday.
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO.
Huang admitted on Sunday to having been 'unfaithful' to his wife.
Reports of an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed.
US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of ties to Chinese intelligence.
China has rejected the allegation that Alice Huang has ties to Chinese intelligence.
Reports on Wednesday described a second alleged affair between Jensen Huang and Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him.
Nvidia's stock market value fell by $550bn over five trading days.
The company says it has no reason to believe trade secrets or national security were compromised.
Nvidia has launched an independent inquiry.
Senator Tim Scott (R-SC), chair of the Senate Banking Committee, summoned both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.
Huang was asked to appear voluntarily on December 3 with a subpoena possible.
Lutnick is set to testify before the same committee in December.
Three House committees (Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, and the Select Committee on China) summoned Huang for a closed-door interview on December 1.
Huang's team told lawmakers he plans to cooperate.
The Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, did not add Megaspeed to its export blacklist despite a classified memo on the concerns.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said other agencies had favored blacklisting the company for months.

The New York Times reported Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce investigators probing Megaspeed by invoking a senior Trump appointee, after which the probe was frozen and handed to the Justice Department.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department has not yet concluded whether Alice Huang engaged in espionage for Beijing.
The White House has told the New York Post that Trump retains 'complete confidence' in Lutnick.
Nvidia makes the advanced chips that power the global AI boom.
Washington has restricted export of advanced chips to China since 2022 over fears they could aid Beijing's military and technological ambitions.
Jensen Huang had unusually close access to President Trump — traveling with him and advocating against the export restrictions he saw as hurting Nvidia's business.

The scandal over Huang's personal relationships, including with a woman US intelligence suspects of Chinese intelligence ties, has intersected with a separate and consequential policy dispute: whether the Commerce Department, under Lutnick, moved too slowly to restrict a company (Megaspeed) suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China, and whether Nvidia's own intervention helped stall that investigation.
What began as a personal scandal has therefore widened into a test of how AI export-control policy is made and enforced at the highest levels of government.

Across party lines, lawmakers and officials agree the core unresolved question is not the affair itself but whether export-control enforcement failed — and who in the administration knew what, and when — making the coming congressional testimony the real test of accountability.

The scheduled December testimony from both Huang and Lutnick, alongside ongoing Justice Department and Nvidia internal investigations, will determine whether this becomes primarily a personal scandal or triggers broader scrutiny of US export-control enforcement and decision-making inside the Trump administration's China policy.

stories.headline: Europe pushes for seat at Ukraine peace talks amid US-Russia diplomacy
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on AP
body: European leaders are scrambling to secure a seat at the table in peace talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin. The US envoys indicated that European representatives would be included in future rounds of negotiations, but the Kremlin has since cast doubt on that, saying no final decision on European participation has been made. The discussions come as Moscow revives its maximalist demands from December 2021, calling for a new European security architecture that would halt NATO's eastward expansion and roll back alliance infrastructure from central and eastern Europe — demands Western leaders previously rejected as an ultimatum.

At an EU summit in Dublin, leaders debated who should represent Europe in the talks, with no consensus yet. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has put herself forward, arguing she is the natural institutional voice for the bloc, but she faces resistance from some who view her as uncompromising on Russia. European Council President Antonio Costa is also a contender, while many national leaders want to attend themselves. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni warned that the absence of a united European voice has allowed freelance diplomacy, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pleaded with the US to avoid surprises, referencing the 'Anchorage moment' when European allies were stunned by US overtures to Russia without Kyiv or Europe present.

Moscow has shown little interest in including Europe, criticizing European leaders for their military support for Ukraine. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that once Russia understands European 'true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format.' Russia's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov has suggested Moscow will add new demands to its list, citing Western efforts to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. The EU's top diplomat Kallas called Russia's push for a new security architecture a 'trap' designed to shift attention from a ceasefire, insisting that the priority should be a ceasefire first, then a peace agreement, and only then discussions on wider European security.

Putin appeared uncompromising and confident during the talks, buoyed by US engagement and recent outreach from European leaders. Russian media have even compared a potential meeting between Putin, US President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen to the 'Big Three' of Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill in 1945. Despite suffering huge battlefield losses and facing economic pressure from Ukrainian drone strikes on its oil refineries, Putin has shown no willingness to end the fighting. Zelenskyy has insisted on European involvement, telling leaders in Dublin that while Europeans are not yet at the table with Russia, they are already involved and must become a regular part of the negotiations.

stories.headline: Global Microsoft outage disrupts Teams, Outlook and other services
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: A major Microsoft outage disrupted services including Teams, Outlook, and AI software Copilot across 74 countries for roughly 18 to 20 hours, beginning late Thursday and continuing into Friday. Microsoft said the issue was a technical problem, not a cyber-security incident, and that it had "addressed the underlying issue" and was gradually restoring services. The company apologized, saying it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners."

The outage affected Microsoft 365 apps used by more than 430 million people, with nearly 130,000 reports of problems logged on the outage website Down Detector. Users experienced varying levels of access: many could not send or receive emails, view files, or use calendar apps, while some could still use Teams without issues. Microsoft attributed the problem to "elevated load" on its infrastructure stemming from an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade. The company warned of continued "intermittent access issues" and delayed email delivery, extending the email timeout window to 48 hours to protect delayed messages.

Experts said the outage's duration was unusually long. Professor James Ferryman of the University of Reading explained that the part of Microsoft's servers that sets up secure connections became swamped, causing a cascading failure: "One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in." He said the fix required bringing services back bit by bit to manage the surge of reconnecting devices. Gergely Orosz, a former software engineer at Skype and Uber, called it potentially the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time."

The disruption had widespread effects. In the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police, and schools were affected; some police forces urged the public to call rather than report crimes online. In the US, congressional offices, the City of Tampa, and law enforcement agencies reported problems; a Colorado sheriff's office said it could not process bond payments via email. Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned of communications delays. In Canada, a Toronto healthcare network experienced email issues but said patient care was not affected. Japan's government reported disruption to its shared IT platform. Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said email support was affected, and Taiwanese financial firms reported disruptions. Tech companies OpenAI and Anthropic also reported problems with their Microsoft connectors.

Microsoft's executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: "We regret that today's outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue." By Friday afternoon, Microsoft reported "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America, with email queues "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels." The company warned that some users might still experience intermittent issues. Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt noted that the outage "reminds us how critical email still is" and affects not only work but also communication about appointments, purchases, and account access. Mark Gregory, an associate professor at RMIT University, said the outage appeared to involve a misconfiguration in the network layer, causing a cascading overload of servers, and advised businesses reliant on cloud services to have backup options.

stories.headline: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over uninspected Iran nuclear site
body: The United Nations nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran that it has not been allowed to inspect. In a quarterly report to member states, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it does not know the exact location of the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP), whether it contains nuclear material, or its status for safeguards purposes. The IAEA described the lack of information as "a matter of serious proliferation concern" that "needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency."

Iran informed the IAEA of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan on 12 June 2025, a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites. The United States joined the strikes later that month. Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after the Israeli attacks began. Since the start of the war, Iran has allowed only very limited IAEA inspections, telling the agency that it is not possible to resume inspections amid the current security situation. Iran later passed a law suspending cooperation with the IAEA, and the watchdog withdrew its inspectors for safety reasons.

The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in the US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above ground; the condition of its underground facilities is not clear. The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there. Before the strikes, Iran had accumulated an estimated 441kg of uranium enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade. Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran had agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity, limits it subsequently exceeded. The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons, something Iran has consistently denied seeking, saying its programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Iran remains committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty but blamed US and Israeli attacks for limiting cooperation with the IAEA. Iran told the IAEA this month that discussion on resuming inspections cannot resume amid "persistent, explicit, and public threats by the President of the United States of America … to commit further acts of armed aggression." Iran said the issue would not be resolved "until the root causes of the present situation are addressed and the essential requirements for normal safeguards implementation are restored." The IAEA said it is "fully prepared to resume its safeguards activities in Iran at short notice" and urged Iran to consider limited technical measures that could make inspection visits possible.

stories.headline: Nvidia scandal: What's next for the US tech company?
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The 63-year-old cofounder and face of the chipmaking giant, valued at nearly $4 trillion, was forced out of the company and off its board. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor. The scandal has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from Nvidia's market value, dragging down the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Nvidia shares lost about 11 percent of their value this week through Thursday, though they rose 1.8 percent in premarket trading on Friday. The company is on course for its longest streak of weekly losses since October 2012.

The scandal began on October 29, when The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and executive associated with Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed International, had been tapped by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information from Jensen Huang. The two were involved in an intimate relationship, which Huang confirmed in an internal memo to Nvidia staff. 'I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,' he wrote. Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The business links extend beyond the affair: Megaspeed purchased more than $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips over roughly two years, and The Information reported that Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, raising questions about possible violations of US export controls. On Wednesday, the NYT reported a second alleged affair between Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. The next day, Reuters reported a third alleged affair with another Nvidia employee.

Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for advanced AI chips used to train frontier AI models, giving it extraordinary influence over the global AI industry. Its customers include tech giants such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, which rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate AI data centres. Washington has restricted Nvidia from selling chips to China, and Huang had spent years lobbying against those restrictions, arguing that they would surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors. A Reuters review identified more than $3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia's restricted processors, underscoring how deeply Nvidia's technology remains embedded in China's AI expansion despite US export controls.

The scandal has also put pressure on US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, the Associated Press reported, after a US intelligence report about Huang's relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior Trump administration officials. Lutnick faces criticism for a delay by the commerce department in adding Megaspeed to Washington's blacklist of companies considered a national security risk, despite reported concerns within the administration. stories.headline: Nvidia stock extends slide as leadership crisis and China scandal deepen
body: Nvidia shares fell for a sixth consecutive week, wiping out $657 billion in market capitalization and extending a losing streak not seen in 14 years. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.2% on Friday as Nvidia's decline weighed on the tech-heavy index, though the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average each posted gains for the week. The company's stock had already fallen 33% from its Oct. 6 peak through Thursday morning, before the latest leg of the slide.

The sell-off accelerated after former CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday, admitting to an extramarital affair with a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and had led it since, had pushed the Trump administration to ease restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department, along with Defense, State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, had for months favored putting Megaspeed on the entity list, but that the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, was responsible for export controls. Bessent told CNBC he was frustrated that "any leakage" of Nvidia chips to China hurts U.S. companies and gives China an advantage, and he questioned whether Nvidia knew its client was a pass-through shell company. Commerce has denied a reported Situation Room confrontation between Bessent and Lutnick over the issue.

Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Huang and Lutnick have both been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, and Huang has been separately invited to a closed-door briefing Dec. 1 before House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast also asked Commerce Under Secretary Jeff Kessler to appear Dec. 3 for a hearing on chip smuggling and alleged interference in export-control enforcement.

The leadership crisis has raised concerns about Nvidia's role as the "central bank of AI," a nickname reflecting the hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments the company has made to support the AI buildout. Nvidia has disclosed obligations including up to $36 billion in cloud-service purchase commitments from neocloud firms, a $105 billion phased guarantee for a data center project in Ohio, and a pledge to backstop up to $125 billion of a $500 billion credit program from Wall Street firms. Columbia Business School finance professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the total at roughly $400 billion, a sum he said remains a small fraction of Nvidia's roughly $3.9 trillion market capitalization even after the stock decline. Analysts expect Nvidia's revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year and roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data.

Regulators and central bankers are closely watching the AI sector for systemic risk. The IMF's Global Financial Stability report in October warned that growing leverage among AI firms and investors could trigger broader problems, and Federal Reserve officials had discussed as early as July the possibility of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of AI-sector trouble. Former FDIC chair Sheila Bair said Nvidia is not "too big to fail in a bank sense" and its equity provides a cushion, but added that "Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event" and that regulators need to watch bank exposure to the company. For now, most neocloud equity prices have recovered this week even as Nvidia shares fell, suggesting investors see the company's problems as specific to it rather than a sector-wide contagion.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang Affair Shifts Outlook for U.S.-China Relations Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit
body: Prolonged U.S. Congressional scrutiny of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises the stakes for already tense relations between the world's two largest economies, according to analysts and officials cited by CNBC. Huang resigned Thursday and agreed to testify before Congress sometime before Thanksgiving on Nov. 26. House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told reporters there could be "public hearings for other people or other things down road."

The affair centers on Huang's relationship with businesswoman Alice Huang, whom U.S. government intelligence believes China's Ministry of State Security recruited to gather information on then-CEO Jensen Huang, according to reports in The Financial Times and The New York Times citing unnamed sources. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair over the weekend. It remains unclear whether any sensitive information was shared. China's Foreign Ministry has called the allegation unfounded "smears against China." Spokeswoman Mao Ning said Thursday, according to an official English translation, "The U.S. should stop fabricating the 'Chinese spy' narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions."

The political landscape has shifted rapidly. Democrats swept U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, followed by turmoil over reports about Huang's alleged Beijing spy connection. At the peak of his influence, Huang shared a banquet table in September with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in Washington, D.C. The two presidents are next expected to meet alongside the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, China. Washington started to restrict Nvidia's ability to sell advanced chips to China in 2022, but the Trump administration eased many Biden-era restrictions in 2025.

"I worry this incident will deteriorate the atmosphere dramatically in Washington against China, and also export control matters, and also the Trump administration in its way of dealing with China," said a Beijing-based foreign policy researcher, who requested anonymity as academics risk discipline or even removal for speaking to the media. The researcher warned of a possible return to a situation like that in the 1990s, when a Chinese-American nuclear physicist was suspected of sharing nuclear secrets with the Chinese government, resulting in a federal prosecution that ultimately dismissed all but one of 59 counts.

"This isn't really about Jensen," said Mitch Presnick, non-resident honorary fellow on the Chinese economy at the Asia Society's Center for China Analysis. He noted how some in Washington prefer measures to exclude China and disagreed with Huang's message that American technology needed to be used in China to remain relevant globally. "The timing is no accident here," Presnick said, pointing to "a very curious set of coincidences" and the fact that information came through unnamed sources. "Obviously somebody was looking to do this, and they wanted to ... make the discussion about espionage, and not about American competitiveness."

"The Nvidia scandal has destroyed the credibility of the biggest corporate lobbyist against U.S. export controls on China," said Arthur Kroeber, partner at Gavekal Dragonomics. "There is now a good chance that Congress will tighten up those rules before the end of this year." Kroeber warned Beijing could cut off supplies of rare earths or chipmaking materials if the U.S. tried to restrict China further with the MATCH Act or Affiliates Rule. "So when Trump and Xi meet next week in Shenzhen they will probably agree to keep the uneasy U.S.-China truce going," Kroeber said. "It will just keep getting more and more uneasy." George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, said, "We are going to see the two countries start to decouple again in terms of technology," adding that "China will double-down on self-reliance." He compared the Huang case to the 2023 "spy balloon" incident, which delayed then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken's trip to China by more than four months.

stories.headline: Fed reduces rate-setting meetings in 2027, October session becomes non-voting
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The Federal Reserve announced Thursday that its October 2027 meeting will not include a vote on interest rates, reducing the number of rate decisions from eight to seven that year. The Federal Open Market Committee will instead dedicate the Oct. 26-27 session to "the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues," with no post-meeting statement or formal vote. The final meeting of 2027 has been moved from December to Nov. 16-17.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who telegraphed the change at his October press conference, said the shift is part of a broader effort to streamline communication and reduce the central bank's market footprint. "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals," Warsh said. "But it's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations—for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons." He indicated that in 2028, two of the eight FOMC meetings would become non-voting strategy sessions.

Warsh has been critical of the Fed's prior communications strategy, arguing that excessive guidance on policy moves handcuffed policymakers. Since he took over, the post-meeting statement has been shortened, and press question-and-answer sessions have been cut to roughly half an hour from the customary 45 minutes. "I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail," Warsh said. "It's an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions."

The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 mandates the FOMC meet at least four times per year. The meeting cadence varied from four to 19 over the years and was set at eight in 1981. Bloomberg reported in September that several regional Fed presidents—including Austan Goolsbee, Beth Hammack, Anna Paulson, and Jeffrey Schmid—had expressed openness to scaling back the rate-setting schedule. The October meeting was chosen for the strategy session in part because it historically preceded federal election cycles, and the Fed has typically avoided rate adjustments at that meeting to avoid the appearance of political motivation—though there have been exceptions, such as the half-point cut in 2024.

The move comes as President Donald Trump continues to call on the Fed to slash interest rates to zero. Warsh, a Trump appointee, has been cagey about the future direction of rates. The Fed raised rates by 25 basis points at its September 2026 meeting, its first hike since 2023, as inflation remains high. U.S. inflation in October reached an annualized rate of 4%, double the Fed's 2% target. Financial markets have priced in a 100% chance of another 25-basis-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. The tentative 2027 FOMC schedule includes meetings on Jan. 26-27, March 16-17, April 27-28, June 8-9, July 27-28, Sept. 14-15, Oct. 26-27 (strategy only), and Nov. 16-17.

stories.headline: Pochettino emotional as he leaves USA for Manchester United job
body: Mauricio Pochettino has been appointed Manchester United head coach, signing a two-and-a-half-year contract after United paid a release clause of approximately £7.4 million to extract him from his role as USA national team boss, with an additional payment for his backroom staff. The 54-year-old Argentine broke down in tears during his first news conference after the move was confirmed, describing the decision to leave the US job as 'one of the most difficult' of his career.

'It's difficult to talk now,' Pochettino said. 'I'm a very emotional guy. It's a very sad decision. But we are professionals and we are trying to make our dreams come true.' Pochettino had signed a new four-year deal with the USA in the summer but will depart after leading the national team in matches against Haiti on 14 and 18 November. Asked why he signed a new deal only to accept United's offer, he said: 'I never said I wanted to go back but they know there aren't too many opportunities that happen in your career like Manchester United. When it arrives, it's difficult to turn down.'

Pochettino replaces Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after United's worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years, leaving the club 18th in the Premier League with just one win in 10 league matches, one point above bottom-placed Sunderland. Carrick released a statement thanking fans for their support, writing: 'I've had the immense privilege of leading Manchester United, the football club that I love. There are very few who get to live that and feel it, and for that I'm incredibly grateful.' Pochettino's first match in charge will be an away match against Liverpool on 22 November.

Pochettino's arrival at Old Trafford marks the end of a decade-long courtship by United. He first came to prominence during an 18-month stint at Southampton, leading them to eighth place in his only full season, before moving to Tottenham in 2014. At Spurs, his reputation rocketed as he led the club to top-four finishes four times in five full seasons — a club that had finished in the top four just twice in the 22 years before his appointment. United first considered a move for Pochettino two years into his time in north London, when he dined with legendary former United boss Sir Alex Ferguson in Mayfair weeks before Louis van Gaal was sacked. The club ultimately appointed Jose Mourinho, then Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, and later Erik ten Hag, before finally hiring Pochettino.

Pochettino has described himself as a 'disciple' of Argentine coach Marcelo Bielsa and has said his sides need 'to be protagonists, always press high, work hard and be dynamic.' He has also expressed deep admiration for Ferguson, naming him as the three Premier League managers he would have loved to have played for. 'When I was young, when I started my career as a manager, he was always my inspiration, my reference,' Pochettino said. United officials have stressed unanimity in the hierarchy regarding the appointment, stating privately that any claim of a split between the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe is 'categorically false.'

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns amid affair, spy probe, and congressional investigations
body: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, ending his 33-year tenure at the helm of the AI chip giant amid a widening scandal involving extramarital affairs, a federal espionage investigation, and congressional inquiries. The resignation came after reports that Huang had affairs with a Chinese executive suspected of being a spy and with at least two Nvidia employees.

According to a TechCrunch timeline, U.S. officials believe that one of Huang's romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation), is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information to Beijing. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years and has been investigated by the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has taken over the federal investigation. Separately, The New York Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Reuters later reported a third affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.

Beyond the personal and national security dimensions, Huang's leadership left a significant environmental footprint. Under his watch, Nvidia's supply-chain emissions grew 725% since 2020, reaching about 10.7 million metric tons of CO2 in fiscal year 2026, according to the company's sustainability report. An analysis by researcher Ketan Joshi and environmental groups estimated that emissions from the use of Nvidia chips could have reached 21 million metric tons in 2025, comparable to Russia's state-owned coal company. Huang had defended AI's environmental cost, comparing it to a surgeon who "has to cut you open to save you," and argued that AI is the best opportunity to address climate change.

Environmental groups have long criticized Nvidia's lack of accountability. Greenpeace East Asia's Avex Li said in a press release that Huang "failed to put climate responsibility at the heart of the company’s growth strategy" and urged interim CEO Colette Kress to commit Nvidia to decarbonizing through renewable energy and ensuring its technology respects human rights. Greenpeace activists disrupted Huang's speech at a Berlin conference last month, and the organization says Nvidia has not met with them despite two years of attempts. Katrin Wu of Greenpeace International stated, "Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues."

The scandal has thrust Nvidia into an unprecedented spotlight just as data centers face growing backlash from communities. Reports indicate that Huang was not confident in his successor, Colette Kress, and described him as "broken." The company's influence on global AI infrastructure and its dealings in China are now under intense scrutiny, with implications for the stability of the AI industry and U.S.-China tech competition. Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge.

stories.headline: Microsoft global outage continues, impacting Outlook and cloud services
body: Microsoft’s massive outage, which began Thursday and disrupted Outlook email, Teams, and a wide range of cloud services worldwide, is slowly recovering as the company works to restore full functionality. The incident, initially reported in the U.S. and the Americas, quickly spread globally, affecting millions of users and knocking out not only email and video conferencing but also Microsoft’s Copilot AI tools, Defender security software, SharePoint Online, and system administrator dashboards. Some users also experienced issues accessing cloud-based Windows computers.

By Friday morning U.S. East Coast time, Microsoft reported that service availability and email delivery performance were improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure. Senior Verge correspondent Tom Warren, citing sources, linked the outage to Azure VNet configuration changes. Microsoft has stated there is no evidence of malicious activity, describing the event as a technical issue unrelated to cyberattacks, AI agents, or DDoS. The company said it continues to investigate the root cause and will share a full report after mitigation.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s Copilot, agents, and platform leader, said in a statement: “We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure. We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us. Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.”

Despite the recovery, some users may still experience intermittent connectivity issues or delayed email delivery, Microsoft said in a status update. Doug Madory, director of internet analysis at Kentik, noted on Bluesky that traffic was returning to Microsoft’s services after about 18 hours of downtime. The outage affected a broad range of industries, including TechCrunch’s own email, and raised questions about Microsoft’s ability to swiftly recover from an incident of its own making.

This is the second major Microsoft cloud outage in recent months. In September, a days-long disruption was attributed to a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing services. Microsoft has not yet provided a detailed explanation for the current outage, and a spokesperson did not respond to questions about whether the company has logs or other means to detect malicious activity. The company has promised a full post-incident review.

stories.headline: Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen for agentic workflows, replacing 3.8 Flash across products
body: Google has released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a new AI model designed for fast, efficient execution across agentic workflows, replacing the previous Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products. The model is rolling out immediately to all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini app, Google Search, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, with access beginning globally for all Search users. Google claims Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than 3.8 Flash at its default high thinking level, reduces fabricated claims by more than five times, and more than triples 3.8 Flash's score on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (57% vs. 18.2%).

Hydrogen offers four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new extra-high tier called xhigh — allowing users to balance quality, latency, and cost. At its high default setting, Hydrogen scored 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, surpassing the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon (50), and reached 54 at the xhigh setting. The model is priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens across its entire 1 million-token context window. On multi-step tasks like deep research and data analysis, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena's live benchmark.

Google positions Hydrogen as a complement to its frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, which are designed for deep, long-horizon reasoning on hard problems. Hydrogen is built for rapid execution in everyday coding, agentic workflows, and multi-model collaboration. To facilitate this, Google introduced Orchestrator in Google Antigravity, which dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while consuming 24% less quota and completing tasks 19% faster on average.

In Google Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements: better understanding of user intent, including handling multi-part queries, highly specific requests, and hard-to-understand typos; more visual responses such as images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools in AI Mode; and an upgraded query fan-out technique that breaks single prompts into multiple subqueries to surface a wider range of relevant links. Google called Hydrogen its 'biggest model improvement to Search yet.'

For developers and enterprise users, Hydrogen excels in iterative repository coding and debugging, open-ended agentic execution, multimodal knowledge work, and web development. It leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks No. 1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for No. 1 on Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA. On the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark, Hydrogen scored 53.4% for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 it scored 71.6% for professional workflows. In early testing with partners, Hydrogen ran 2x to 2.8x faster than 3.8 Flash while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%.

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen improves multi-turn conversations by better following user guidance, calling the right tools, and producing reliable outputs with less back-and-forth. It can pull context from uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and connected apps like Airtable and Dropbox. Google says Hydrogen is designed to stand on its own for everyday work or to pair with Carbon and Argon as a high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
